summary_html: Court issues a **protective or restraining order** to prevent contact, remove abuser, or ensure safety without removing the child. Federal law leaves implementation to states but funds protection efforts through CAPTA and IV-B.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — authorizes protective interventions and state plan requirements  
- **SSA Title IV-B** — permits funding for protective services and court interventions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed a youth court's abuse adjudication and custody order because the father was never served or notified of the hearings and the court did not comply with the Youth Court Act's notice and advice-of-rights requirements.
key_cases.relevance: The youth court's protective response was to place the child with the non-offending mother after finding abuse by the father, the Mississippi alternative to removal.
key_cases.quote: The Hinds County Youth Court failed to comply with the statutory requirements to assure notice to the father for the various hearings affecting the custody of his minor son

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment on qualified-immunity grounds, the court held prospectively that the Fourth Amendment governs child-abuse investigations, that the government may not seize a child absent a court order, parental consent or exigent circumstances, and that an uncorroborated anonymous tip will rarely justify seizing a child.
key_cases.relevance: A court order is the ordinary lawful instrument for protective intervention; its absence must be justified by consent or exigency.
key_cases.quote: an anonymous tip regarding child abuse will rarely be sufficient to justify the seizure of a child

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the caseworker who removed two boys not named in the court order and with no evidence of imminent danger, holding that requirement was clearly established before Gates, while reversing as to the search and the supervisor.
key_cases.relevance: A court order authorizing action as to one child does not authorize seizure of that child's siblings.
key_cases.quote: Gates was not required to give social workers fair notice that imminent danger must exist before a child may be removed without a warrant or court order

Code § 43-21-309(1), https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-43/chapter-21/custody-and-detention/section-43-21-309/)
